title: Most people preach Martha like she was the villain of the story.
paragraphs: Most people preach Martha like she was the villain of the story.

Busy.
Distracted.
Too focused on work.
Too earthly.
Too anxious.
And Mary becomes the spiritual hero because she sat quietly at the feet of Jesus.
But when you actually slow down and study the text carefully in its original language… something shocking appears.
Martha was not rebuked for serving.
She was breaking under pressure while trying to honor Jesus the best way she knew how.
And that changes everything.
Because some of you reading this are Martha right now.

You love God.
You’re trying.
You serve everybody.
You carry responsibilities nobody notices.
You keep the house together emotionally, spiritually, financially.
You’re exhausted while everyone else seems peaceful.

And secretly…
you wonder if Jesus is disappointed in you too.
But the story is far deeper than most sermons make it sound.
The account appears in Gospel of Luke 10:38–42.
The Greek text says:

“Ἡ δὲ Μάρθα περιεσπᾶτο περὶ πολλὴν διακονίαν”
Hē de Martha periespato peri pollēn diakonian
Most English translations say:
“Martha was distracted with much serving.”
But the word “περιεσπᾶτο” (periespato) is incredibly important.
It does not simply mean “busy.”

It carries the idea of being:
dragged away,
pulled apart,
emotionally overextended,
mentally torn in different directions.
Martha was not merely working.
She was internally unraveling.

And honestly…
that sounds like many believers today.

Smiling publicly.
Falling apart privately.

Still attending church.
Still posting Bible verses.
Still helping everybody.
Still answering messages.
Still cooking.
Still serving.
Still functioning.

But internally?
Being pulled apart by pressure.
The tragedy is that modern Christianity often glorifies exhaustion while pretending it is holiness.
Martha welcomed Jesus into her home.
Do not miss that.
The text first says:

“ὑπεδέξατο αὐτὸν”
hypedexato auton
“She welcomed Him.”

This was hospitality.
Honor.
Love.
In first-century Jewish culture, hospitality was sacred.
Especially toward a rabbi.
Martha was likely trying to prepare food, organize the home, care for guests, maintain honor, and fulfill cultural expectations all at once.
She was not being sinful by serving.
In fact, the Greek word for “serving” is:

“διακονία”
diakonia
The same root used later for ministry and service in the church.
The same root connected to deacons.
The same kind of service Jesus Himself honored.
So Jesus was not condemning work.
He was exposing anxiety-driven distraction.
There is a massive difference.
Some people use this story to shame hardworking believers.

But Jesus never said:
“Martha, stop serving.”
He said:

“Μάρθα Μάρθα, μεριμνᾷς καὶ θορυβάζῃ περὶ πολλά”
Martha, Martha, merimnas kai thorubazē peri polla
Usually translated:
“You are anxious and troubled about many things.”
The word “μεριμνᾷς” (merimnas) means anxious, divided by cares, mentally consumed.
The word “θορυβάζῃ” (thorubazē) means inward turmoil, disturbance, noisy agitation.

Jesus was addressing her condition…
not attacking her character.
That matters deeply.
Because many exhausted Christians think God is angry at them for being overwhelmed.
But Jesus spoke to Martha tenderly.
Notice He says her name twice.
“Martha, Martha…”
In Hebrew culture, repetition of a name communicated affection, grief, and intimacy.
Like:

“Abraham, Abraham.”
“Moses, Moses.”
“Simon, Simon.”
This was not public humiliation.
This was compassion.
Jesus saw a woman drowning internally while trying to do everything right.
And some of you know exactly what that feels like.

You pray while multitasking.
You worship while emotionally numb.
You serve while secretly exhausted.
You help everybody while nobody asks how you’re doing.

And eventually…
your service to God becomes separated from closeness with God.
That is the danger Martha faced.
Not serving.
Serving without rest in His presence.

Mary chose “the better portion,” not because work was evil…
but because intimacy must come before activity.
The Greek phrase is:

“τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα”
tēn agathēn merida
“the good portion”
“Merida” means portion, share, nourishment.
This language echoes ancient covenant meals and even Psalmic imagery.
Like Book of Psalms 16:5:
“The Lord is my chosen portion…”

Mary recognized something Martha was forgetting in the pressure:
Jesus Himself was the portion.

Not performance.
Not perfection.
Not proving yourself useful.
Him.
And this is where the story becomes painfully modern.

Many believers today know ministry…
but not stillness.

They know church activity…
but not communion.

They know how to post sermons…
but not how to sit quietly with God when nobody is watching.
And eventually the soul begins starving while the schedule stays full.
Martha loved Jesus.
Do not let shallow preaching convince you otherwise.
In fact, one of the most beautiful moments in all of Scripture happens later in Gospel of John 11 during the death of Lazarus.
Who runs toward Jesus with one of the greatest confessions of faith ever spoken?
Martha.
Not Mary.
Martha says:

“ναί κύριε, ἐγὼ πεπίστευκα”
nai kyrie, egō pepisteuka
“Yes Lord, I have believed…”
Then she declares:

“σὺ εἶ ὁ Χριστός”
sy ei ho Christos
“You are the Christ.”
This is profound.
The same Martha people reduce to “the distracted woman” was actually a woman of deep faith.
Jesus loved Martha.
The text explicitly says in John 11:5:

“ἠγάπα δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὴν Μάρθαν”
ēgapa de ho Iēsous tēn Marthan
“Jesus loved Martha.”

Not tolerated.
Loved.
Some of you need to hear that clearly.

Jesus does not only love the peaceful Christians.
The emotionally composed Christians.
The believers who always seem spiritually calm.
He also loves the overwhelmed ones.

The anxious ones.
The mentally exhausted ones.
The believers barely holding themselves together.
The issue was never that Martha served.
The issue was that her anxiety pulled her away from the very Person she was serving.

And if we are honest…
many of us have done the exact same thing.
We become so consumed with surviving life that we stop sitting with Jesus Himself.

We panic.
Rush.
Scroll endlessly.
Numb ourselves with noise.
Stay constantly stimulated because silence forces us to face what’s happening inside.
But Jesus still says:
“There is one thing necessary.”

Not one hundred things.
Not endless striving.
Not spiritual performance.
One thing.
Presence before productivity.
Communion before chaos.
Christ before everything else.
And maybe the reason this story still hurts people so deeply is because they see themselves in Martha.

Not rebellious.
Not evil.
Just tired.

Tired of carrying everything.
Tired of trying to hold life together.
Tired of serving while silently breaking inside.
But Jesus never stopped loving Martha.
And He has not stopped loving you either.
Somebody reading this has been confusing exhaustion with failure.
But God is not asking you to earn His love through endless striving.
He is calling you close again.

Not just to work for Him…
but to be with Him.
Because eventually your soul cannot survive on activity alone.
It needs the presence of Christ.

And maybe tonight…
before another sermon,
another scroll,
another distraction,
another attempt to hold yourself together…
you need to sit at His feet again.
Not as a failure.
But as someone deeply loved by Jesus.
Somebody you know is silently carrying more than they admit.

You can be deeply overwhelmed…
and still deeply loved by Christ.
